P1_fx_receipts.question: Can resident individuals receive foreign currency for services or digital exports? Any conversion or repatriation rule?
P1_fx_receipts.answer: Yes, freely. BSP's Manual of Regulations on Foreign Exchange Transactions says residents may use FX receipts, acquisitions or earnings from non-trade sources (services count here) freely for any purpose. At their option they may sell them for pesos, keep them, or deposit them in foreign-currency accounts in the Philippines or abroad. There is no surrender or mandatory conversion.

P2_fcy_account.question: Can individuals hold a foreign-currency bank account?
P2_fcy_account.answer: Yes. Residents may keep FX earnings or deposit them in foreign-currency accounts in the Philippines or abroad (BSP FX Manual). Banks operate Foreign Currency Deposit Units (FCDUs and EFCDUs) for this.

P5_payoneer_wise.question: Payoneer / Wise availability for residents
P5_payoneer_wise.answer: Both available. L1_registration.question: Must an individual selling digital products or services register a business? How (sole proprietor), cost, online?
L1_registration.answer: Yes, with BIR. BIR's Taxpayer's Guide for Online Sellers covers ALL online sellers 'doing business and earning income in any manner or form' through electronic platforms or their own website. They register with BIR as individuals (Form 1901) online via ORUS, or at the Revenue District Office, and pay ₱30 documentary stamp tax. A DTI business-name certificate is needed only if you use a business name: DTI defines that as any name different from your true name used in the business. DTI registration is online (BNRS). Local mayor's permits were not researched.

L3_income_tax_foreign.question: How residents' foreign-sourced or digital income is taxed
L3_income_tax_foreign.answer: A Filipino citizen residing in the Philippines is taxed on all income from sources inside and outside the Philippines (NIRC s.23(A)). Self-employed people and professionals whose gross sales or receipts don't exceed the ₱3,000,000 VAT threshold can choose an 8% tax on gross sales or receipts above ₱250,000, instead of graduated income tax rates AND the percentage tax. They elect it at registration (Form 1901) or on the first quarterly return; VAT-registered taxpayers can't use it. Otherwise graduated rates apply (Sec. 24(A)(2)(a)).

L4_vat_gst.question: VAT/GST rate, registration threshold, treatment of exported services and digital services
L4_vat_gst.answer: VAT registration threshold: ₱3,000,000 in gross sales or receipts. Below it, self-employed people pay percentage tax under s.116 unless they chose the 8% option, which replaces both. For VAT-registered persons, services paid for in acceptable foreign currency and accounted for under BSP rules are zero-rated (NIRC s.108(B)). BIR's RMC 059-2026 (2 June 2026) reaffirmed that services by a Philippine entity to a nonresident foreign corporation are zero-rated under those conditions (KPMG summary). Since RA 12023 (RR 3-2025), FOREIGN digital service providers charge 12% VAT to Philippine customers; that affects buyers, not local exporters.

L5_data_protection.question: Data-protection law: name, year, in force?, regulator
L5_data_protection.answer: Data Privacy Act of 2012 (Republic Act No. 10173), which created the National Privacy Commission (NPC). Anyone who controls the collection, holding, processing or use of personal information is a 'personal information controller', and that includes a person instructing others to process data for them.

L6_consumer_ecommerce.question: E-commerce / consumer-protection law relevant to online sales
L6_consumer_ecommerce.answer: Internet Transactions Act of 2023 (RA 11967). It applies to B2B and B2C internet transactions within DTI's mandate where one party is in the Philippines, or where the online merchant targets the Philippine market and has minimum contacts there. Online media content and consumer-to-consumer transactions are excluded. An 'online merchant' is anyone selling non-financial goods or services to online consumers through e-marketplaces or third-party platforms. The Act creates a DTI E-Commerce Bureau. It also sets up an Online Business Database and an E-Commerce Philippine Trustmark (KPMG). A secondary source says the Act took full effect on 20 June 2025 after an 18-month transition (not verified).

L7_incentives.answer: (1) The 8% optional income tax on gross receipts above ₱250,000, for those within the ₱3m threshold: no percentage tax and simple computation (L3). D1_id_document.question: Name of the national identity document residents use for identity checks
D1_id_document.answer: The Philippine Identification (PhilID) under the Philippine Identification System (PhilSys), RA 11055. Its purpose is a valid proof of identity for all citizens and resident aliens; an ePhilID digital version also exists. Banks and remittance centres accept it.

W1_workarounds.question: Simple, legal routes around payment barriers for a beginner (no misrepresentation, nominees or sanctions evasion)
W1_workarounds.answer: Barriers: Stripe does not accept merchants here. Simple legal routes: (1) Sell digital products or software through a merchant of record: Paddle (software/SaaS only; each seller reviewed), Lemon Squeezy (bank payouts), Polar, Dodo Payments. The platform is the legal seller to your customers, handles card payments and consumer VAT/sales tax, and pays you out. You still declare the payouts as your income at home (see L3). (2) Sell services on Upwork, which is available here (not on its restricted list). Which withdrawal methods you get (bank, PayPal, Payoneer, etc.) depends on the country and shows in your account. (3) Creator income through the YouTube Partner Program (available here). (4) Paid apps and in-app sales through Google Play (merchant registration available here). (5) Physical or digital goods on Etsy (Etsy seller payments are available here). (6) Client payments by PayPal (on PayPal's Payouts list as 'Send, receive, and withdraw in local currency'). (7) For direct clients, a bank transfer (SWIFT) into your own local account always works. Follow the local foreign-exchange rules (see P1) and keep invoices. (8) Local official channel: Residents may keep foreign-currency earnings in FCDU accounts (BSP FX Manual), and both Wise and Payoneer are available (P2/P5). Avoid: opening accounts with a foreign address, a relative's or friend's identity, or a VPN to look like you are elsewhere. It breaches platform terms (accounts and funds get frozen) and can break anti-money-laundering or sanctions law.
